This homework comes right after the sessions on seasonal decomposition, STL and MSTL. Read all the
instructions before you start.

##### why homework? {.unnumbered}

This is where you build intuition: you will play with parameters and get surprised by what the
data tells you. Doing the homework is **essential to prepare for the exams**. In the exams there
will be no computations. I will show you a series or a decomposition and ask you to reason about
it, and the questions will be variations of what you do here. Homework is the training, the exam
is the match.

Read the [AI policy](/basics/AI-policy.html) before you start. AI is welcome here, but **write

##### where to spend your time {.unnumbered}

Not all effort is equal. For every obstacle you meet, ask yourself: is this **productive
friction** or **pointless friction**?

- *Productive:* sketching what you expect a component to look like, understanding why a
  decomposition behaves the way it does, working out what a graph is telling you.
- *Pointless:* fighting with axis labels, colors or tick formats, an obscure error message,
  remembering the name of an argument.

Spend your time on the first kind, and get help for the second (AI, a classmate, a quick search).
A clear graph is enough, nobody needs a beautiful one. If you have been stuck on the same
cosmetic detail for 15 minutes, move on.
:::

## the data

Use the temperature of the station and the year of the previous homeworks. In the lectures, the
seasonal cycle was the **annual** cycle of sea surface temperature. With one year of data you
cannot study an annual cycle (why not? see part 6), but you can study the **daily** cycle: the
period is one day, and the "typical year" becomes a "typical day".

Download this <a href="/homework/HW-seasonality-template.ipynb" download>Jupyter Notebook
template</a>. It loads your data, averages it to **hourly** values (so one period is 24 data
points), and fills short gaps by interpolation. Check how many values were filled: if your
station has gaps longer than a day or two in the month you choose for parts 1-3, choose another
month.

## how to work

For every graph below, do these three steps, in this order:

1. **Predict.** Before running anything, **sketch on paper** what you expect to see (a quick
   sketch, not a work of art), and describe it in one or two sentences in the notebook. The exam
   will ask you to reason this way, so this is training.
2. **Run.** Make the graph.
3. **Explain.** Compare what you got with what you predicted. If you were surprised, find out why.

A wrong prediction is not a mistake, it is where the learning happens. Please do not edit your
prediction after the fact.

## part 1: a typical day, from scratch

Choose one month of hourly temperature. Decompose it with the same steps we used in [seasonal
decomposition from scratch](/seasonality/seasonal-decomposition-from-scratch.ipynb), but with a
period of one day instead of one year:

1. **trend:** a centered rolling mean with a window of 24 hours;
2. **detrended** = temperature - trend;
3. **seasonal:** the average of the detrended data for each hour of the day (0, 1, ..., 23),
   repeated every day;
4. **residual** = detrended - seasonal.

- **Predict:** sketch the seasonal component for one typical day. At what hour do you expect the
  minimum, and at what hour the maximum? How large is the difference between them (peak to peak)?
- **Explain:** plot the four components (temperature, trend, seasonal, residual) in four panels,
  and also one day of the seasonal component. Were you right? The sun is highest at noon and
  lowest at midnight. Why do the warmest and coldest hours of the typical day not coincide with
  these times?

**What if...** you compute the trend with a window of 18 hours instead of 24? Predict what the
trend will look like, then plot both trends together. Why does the window have to be exactly one
period long (or a whole number of periods)?

<details>
<summary>hint</summary>
```{.python}
temp = hourly.loc['2024-07']
trend = temp.rolling(24, center=True).mean()
detrended = temp - trend
typical_day = detrended.groupby(detrended.index.hour).mean()   # 24 values
seasonal = pd.Series(detrended.index.hour, index=detrended.index).map(typical_day)
residual = detrended - seasonal
```
</details>

## part 2: did it work?

A decomposition always produces a residual, even when it went wrong. How can you check that the
daily cycle is really gone from your residual? If it is still there, then each hour is similar to
the same hour one day earlier.

- **Predict:** what value do you expect for the autocorrelation of the *detrended* series at a lag
  of one day? And for the *residual*?
- **Explain:** compute both (with `.autocorr(lag)`, choosing the right lag). Were you right? Is the
  residual's autocorrelation at this lag exactly zero? Why might it not be?

**What if...** you had kept the original 10-minute data instead of hourly averages? What lag would
you need for the same check? Now compute the autocorrelation at lag 1 of the temperature itself,
once for the hourly data and once for the 10-minute data of the same month. Predict which one is
larger before you run it. What does this tell you about reading a "lag-1 autocorrelation" without knowing
the time step?

<details>
<summary>hint</summary>
```{.python}
print(detrended.autocorr(24), residual.autocorr(24))
```
</details>

## part 3: the same, with statsmodels

Decompose the same month with `seasonal_decompose`, using `period=24`.

- **Predict:** will the seasonal component be the same as yours? Where in the series do you expect
  the two decompositions to differ?
- **Explain:** plot your seasonal component and the `statsmodels` one together, and also the two
  trends. How close are they? Look at the beginning and end of the month: what happens there, in
  both methods, and why?

**What if...** you remove the missing values with `.dropna()` instead of filling them, and then
run `seasonal_decompose` on the shortened series? Choose a month that has some missing hours in
the raw data (or delete a few hours yourself). Predict what will happen to the typical day, then
try it. Why is this dangerous, and why doesn't `seasonal_decompose` warn you?

<details>
<summary>hint</summary>
```{.python}
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose
result = seasonal_decompose(temp, period=24)
result.seasonal, result.trend   # pandas Series, same index as temp
```
</details>

## part 4: does the typical day change through the year?

Our decomposition from scratch assumes one fixed typical day for the whole period. Over a full
year that is hard to believe. Use STL on the **whole year** of hourly temperature, with
`period=24`.

- **Predict:** sketch how the size of the daily cycle (peak to peak, in °C) changes from January to
  December at your station. In which season do you expect the largest daily swing, and why?
- **Explain:** run STL with `seasonal=7`. For each day, compute the peak-to-peak size of the
  seasonal component, and plot it for the whole year. Were you right? Do you see periods of a few
  days or weeks that stand out? What kind of weather could cause them?

**What if...** you use `seasonal=7`, `seasonal=31` and `seasonal=181`? Plot the three daily swings
together. Remember that `seasonal` is measured in number of cycles, here days. What does each one
"listen to," and which would you choose to answer the question in the title?

<details>
<summary>hint</summary>
```{.python}
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
res = STL(hourly, period=24, seasonal=7).fit()
daily_swing = res.seasonal.resample('D').agg(lambda x: x.max() - x.min())
```
</details>

## part 5: a cycle that isn't there

MSTL needs you to tell it the periods. What happens if you ask for one that doesn't exist?
Temperature has a daily cycle, but we have no strong reason to expect a weekly one. The week is a
human convention, and its effect on the weather (for example, less traffic and pollution on
weekends in big cities) is small at best.

- **Predict:** run MSTL on the whole year of hourly temperature with `periods=(24, 24*7)`. Sketch
  what you expect the weekly component (`seasonal_168`) to look like. How large will it be compared
  with the daily component?
- **Explain:** plot both seasonal components for a few weeks, and compare their sizes (for example,
  their standard deviations). Is the weekly component zero? If not, where does it come from?
  Weather systems (a cold front, a heat wave) typically last a few days: how could they end up in a
  "weekly" component?

**What if...** you were analyzing hourly electricity demand in a city instead? Would you expect a
real weekly cycle there? How would you convince a skeptic that a weekly component you found is
real, and not the kind of artifact you just saw?

<details>
<summary>hint</summary>
```{.python}
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import MSTL
res = MSTL(hourly, periods=(24, 24*7)).fit()
res.seasonal['seasonal_24'], res.seasonal['seasonal_168']
```
</details>

## part 6: think like in the exam

Answer in your own words, in a few sentences each. No code is needed for this part, but you can
use your own graphs as evidence.

1. A colleague has exactly one year of daily temperature, and wants to extract its annual seasonal
   component and its trend using a 365-day rolling mean. What will they get? What is the minimum
   amount of data they need, and how much would you recommend?
1. The typical North Atlantic year is coldest in early March and warmest at the end of August
   (see [circling back](/seasonality/circling-back.ipynb)), and in part 1 you found the warmest
   and coldest hours of your typical day. Explain both delays with one physical idea.
1. Would a multiplicative model make sense for temperature in °C? What would a seasonal factor of
   1.2 mean on a day when the trend is 0.5 °C? And on a day when it is -2 °C? What property must a
   quantity have for a multiplicative model to make sense?
1. Global radiation is zero every night, and its midday peak is much higher in summer than in
   winter. Which model, additive or multiplicative, describes its daily cycle better? Why does
   `seasonal_decompose(..., model="multiplicative")` refuse to run on it?
1. A colleague decomposes monthly data with `period=12`, finds that the residual has a lag-1
   autocorrelation of 0.6, and concludes that the decomposition failed. Is lag 1 the right thing to
   look at to judge whether the seasonal component was removed? What would you check instead?
1. The decomposition from scratch gives one fixed seasonal pattern, while STL allows it to evolve.
   Give an example of a series for which this difference matters, and one for which it doesn't.

- Download a second (or third) year of hourly temperature for your station, and run MSTL with
  `periods=(24, 24*365)`. Plot the annual component. Does the daily component change compared with

- Decompose one month of global radiation with STL, once directly and once on

## guidelines

A graph is good enough when it has:

1. a title, and named axes with units;
1. readable tick labels;
1. a legend, if there is more than one line;
1. a size that lets you see everything clearly.
